narrative:
The model determined that you have a 66.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile in both your first and third years of law school placed you far below the average student who was admitted (who typically ranked around the 6th decile). These low rankings signaled to the model a consistent pattern of academic struggle that outweighed other information.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction toward passing. At 3.60 it sits noticeably above the 3.23 average of accepted students. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 31 was also below the accepted average of 37, adding further concern, though it carried less weight than your law school performance. Your family income, gender, race, and full-time status played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
